props.title: Lust, Caution
props.initialSlug: Espionage and passion collide in 1940s Shanghai

sections.content: **Lust, Caution** (2007) represents Ang Lee's most daring exploration of espionage, desire, and political intrigue. Set in Japanese-occupied Shanghai during WWII, the film follows Wong Chia Chi (Tang Wei) as she infiltrates the life of Mr. Yee (Tony Leung), a powerful collaborator. The film's explicit scenes caused controversy, but they're integral to understanding the complex power dynamics. Lee builds on themes he explored in **Brokeback Mountain** (2005), examining how passion can both liberate and destroy. The film's meticulous attention to 1940s period detail rivals that of **The Conformist** (1970). In the Mood for Love|2000|Wong Kar-wai's masterpiece about repressed desire in 1960s Hong Kong|Criterion Black Book|2006|Paul Verhoeven's WWII thriller about a Jewish spy seducing a Nazi officer|Prime The Handmaiden|2016|Park Chan-wook's erotic psychological thriller set in Japanese-occupied Korea|Prime

Tang Wei's devastating performance anchors the film's exploration of identity and betrayal. Like **Notorious** (1946), where Ingrid Bergman's character must seduce a Nazi sympathizer, Wong Chia Chi loses herself in her role. The mahjong scenes crackle with tension reminiscent of the card games in **Casino Royale** (2006), where every gesture carries hidden meaning. Tony Leung brings the same smoldering intensity he showed in **In the Mood for Love** (2000), but here it's tinged with genuine menace.

Ang Lee's direction shows remarkable restraint despite the film's explicit content. He draws influence from classic spy noir like **The Third Man** (1949) while incorporating the psychological complexity of modern Asian cinema. The film's shocking violence serves as punctuation marks in an otherwise elegantly composed narrative, similar to the approach in **A History of Violence** (2005). The film's controversial intimate scenes serve a deeper purpose than mere shock value. Like in **Basic Instinct** (1992) or **Body Heat** (1981), sex becomes a battlefield where power dynamics play out. Lee frames these encounters with the same precision he brought to the martial arts sequences in **Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon** (2000), treating them as choreographed expressions of character development rather than exploitation.
